plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels — (a), (b), and (c) — that together explain how the selective absorption of visible light by a substance determines its perceived color. Panel (a) shows four flat surfaces interacting with multicolored arrows representing the full visible spectrum: the top-left black surface absorbs all incoming colored arrows and reflects none; the top-right white/gray surface reflects all incoming colors; the bottom-left yellow surface absorbs most colors and reflects only yellow; and the bottom-right yellow surface absorbs the complementary color (indigo) from white light, also appearing yellow, illustrating that a color can arise either from selective reflection or from complementary-color absorption. Panel (b) is a color wheel divided into pie-shaped sectors spanning from approximately 400 nm (violet) through 430 nm (blue-violet), 490 nm (cyan-green), 560 nm (yellow-green), 580 nm (yellow), 620 nm (orange-red), and 800 nm (red), with colors arranged so that complementary pairs sit directly across the wheel from each other. Panel (c) depicts a test tube containing a blue [Cu(NH3)4]2+ solution: a full set of colored arrows labeled "White light" enters from the left, the orange and red arrows are absorbed by the solution, and the remaining arrows — violet, blue, cyan, green, and yellow — emerge on the right as "Blue-appearing light." This figure motivates the use of the complementary color wheel to predict what color a transition-metal complex will appear based on which wavelengths its d–d or charge-transfer transitions absorb.

demo_steps.title: Absorption on the wheel
demo_steps.narration: Start on the color wheel with absorption near 620 nm, in the orange-red region. The marker opposite it indicates the complementary blue/cyan appearance.

demo_steps.title: Colored surface
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the surface panel. For a colored yellow-appearing surface, most colors are absorbed while yellow-related light is reflected toward the viewer.

demo_steps.title: Black, white, and transparent limits
demo_steps.narration: Changing the surface type shows the limiting cases: black absorbs all visible bands, white reflects them all, and a transparent material transmits them through the plate.

demo_steps.title: Blue-appearing solution
demo_steps.narration: In the test tube, orange-red absorption removes those wavelengths from white light. The transmitted mixture is dominated by shorter wavelengths and appears blue.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Overall scene should preserve the textbook layout but use a tabbed/panel view by default: panel (b) centered first, with optional linked overview arranging (a) left, (b) upper right, and (c) lower center. Use orthographic/axonometric styling with no strong perspective convergence. Panel (a): one active tilted rectangular plate about 3.2 × 2.0 world units, lying in the XZ plane with +X screen-right and +Z receding up-right; plate corners form a parallelogram like the source. Incoming arrows are parallel colored lines about 2.4 units long, slanting from left/front toward the plate, ordered top-to-bottom violet #4b00ff, blue #1e3cff, cyan #49e6e6, green #33ff00, yellow #ffe600, orange #ff7a00, red #ff0000. Arrowheads point into the plate. Reflected arrows bend at the plate and travel up-right/back-right; transmitted arrows continue through in the same direction for the transparent case. Plate colors: black absorbing #000000; white reflecting #f5f5f5 with gray outline #808080; transparent plate pale gray/white with opacity about 0.25 and gray outline; colored surface pale yellow #ffff66 with gray outline. Colored-surface behavior should by default show yellow/orange-green reflected for yellow appearance and the complementary absorbed wavelength highlighted according to the slider. Panel (b): circular color wheel radius about 1.35 units, flat in screen plane. Divide into approximate sectors following the source labels: 400 nm violet at left-upper-left, 430 nm blue-violet at lower-left, 490 nm cyan at bottom, 560 nm green/yellow-green at lower-right, 580 nm yellow at right-upper-right, 620 nm orange-red at top, 800 nm red at upper-left. Complementary colors lie diametrically opposite; selected wavelength angle should interpolate continuously around this wheel rather than jump only at labels. Use black outlines #000000, label text black. Panel (c): test tube centered vertically, glass cylinder about 0.75 units wide and 3.1 units tall with rounded bottom and elliptical rim; glass pale cyan #b7d9d9 at 0.35 opacity, outlines #88b6b6. Liquid fills lower about 2.2 units, blue #3f86ff with slight vertical gradient and opacity about 0.75. Incoming arrows on left are horizontal, length about 2.0 units, stacked vertically with same visible-spectrum colors, arrowheads pointing right into tube. Outgoing arrows on right are horizontal, length about 2.1 units, with absorbed wavelength and neighboring band attenuated or absent; for wavelength 620 nm, suppress red/orange and leave violet/blue/cyan/green/yellow so the label reads 'Blue-appearing light'. Text labels are black sans-serif and placed as in the source: 'White light' above left bundle and apparent-color label above right bundle.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement the three panels as grouped objects that can be shown/hidden by panelView; in Linked overview scale each group down and place them in the source-like arrangement. The wavelength slider should update a single shared selectedWavelength state: move the color-wheel marker, recolor/brighten the matching arrow, compute complementary apparent hue by adding 180 degrees on the wheel, and update the test-tube liquid and outgoing-arrow mixture. For the click interaction, raycast color wheel sectors and set selectedWavelength to that sector center. Use emissive or high-saturation materials for arrows so the spectrum remains vivid against white background. Render arrows as THREE.Line or TubeGeometry shafts with cone arrowheads; use dashed or fading segments inside surfaces/tube to indicate absorption. Keep all labels as screen-facing sprites or CSS2D text for readability.

authoredContext:
The human eye perceives a mixture of all the colors, in the proportions present in sunlight, as white light. Complementary colors, those located across from each other on a color wheel, are also used in color vision. The eye perceives a mixture of two complementary colors, in the proper proportions, as white light. Likewise, when a color is missing from white light, the eye sees its complement. For example, when red photons are absorbed from white light, the eyes see the color green. When violet photons are removed from white light, the eyes see lemon yellow. The blue color of the [Cu(NH 3 ) 4 ] 2+ ion results because this ion absorbs orange and red light, leaving the complementary colors of blue and green ( ).

(a) An object is black if it absorbs all colors of light. If it reflects all colors of light, it is white. An object has a color if it absorbs all colors except one, such as this yellow strip. The strip also appears yellow if it absorbs the complementary color from white light (in this case, indigo). (b) Complementary colors are located directly across from one another on the color wheel. (c) A solution of [Cu(NH 3 ) 4 ] 2+ ions absorbs red and orange light, so the transmitted light appears as the complementary color, blue.

This figure includes three diagrams. In a, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet incident arrows point from the upper left to the lower right toward one black, one white, and two yellow rectangular surfaces. No arrows are indicated leaving the black surface. On the white surface, arrows of all included colors extend from the surface of the rectangle extending from just right of the tips of the incident arrows that approach the rectangle to the upper right. For the first yellow surface, only a yellow arrow extends from a point just past the tip of the yellow incident arrow to the upper right. For the second yellow surface, all colors of arrows except indigo extend from points just past the tips of the incident arrows to the upper right. In b, a circle shaded in red at the upper left blends to orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet moving clockwise about the circle. The leftmost side of the red region has a radius that is labeled, “800 n m,” at the edge of the circle. A radius drawn to the top of the circle in the red-orange region is labeled, “620 n m.” A radius drawn to a point near the center of the first quadrant of the circle in the orange-yellow region is labeled, “580 n m.” A radius drawn to a point near the center of the second quadrant of the circle in the yellow-green region is labeled, “560 n m.” A radius drawn to the bottom of the circle in the blue region is labeled, “490 n m.” A radius drawn to a point near the center of the third quadrant of the circle in the indigo region is labeled, “430 n m.” An unlabeled radius is drawn to the leftmost point on the circle in the violet region. The violet region ends where the red region began on the circle. This radius is labeled, “400 n m,” just to the left and below the, “800 n m,” label associated with the red region. In c, a test tube containing a blue substance is shown. To the left of the test tube, incident colored arrows are shown pointing to the test tube. The colors of the arrows in order from bottom to top are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Above these arrows is the label, “White light.” To the right of the test tube, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet arrows point right. These arrows are positioned at the same level on the test tube as their matching incident arrows on the left of the test tube. Above these arrows is the label, “Blue-appearing light.”

Small changes in the relative energies of the orbitals that electrons are transitioning between can lead to drastic shifts in the color of light absorbed. Therefore, the colors of coordination compounds depend on many factors. As shown in , different aqueous metal ions can have different colors. In addition, different oxidation states of one metal can produce different colors, as shown for the vanadium complexes in the link below.

discrepancies: The source shows all three panels in a fixed textbook layout, with panel (a) containing four separate surface cases; the generated view defaults to a small overlapped/combined scene and only provides one switchable surface case at a time.
Panel (a) is missing the 2x2 arrangement of black, transparent/outline, yellow reflecting, and yellow transmitting surfaces; it replaces these with a single controllable plate.
The color wheel is not presented as a clean, front-facing standalone circular diagram in the screenshot; it is overlaid with surface arrows, a plate, and the test tube, making panel (b) hard to read.
The test tube panel should be upright and separated below the other panels, but the generated tube is tilted/embedded in the overlapped scene rather than matching the source composition.
For the test-tube concept, the source removes orange/red components from the transmitted light, while the generated absorption model would allow the 800 nm red ray to pass for 620 nm absorption.
The generated figure adds extra titles, markers, pointer lines, legends, chemical labels, and annotations that are not present in the source and clutter the textbook-style diagram.
evaluation.notes: The generated scene includes the right general topics and useful controls, but the layout, panel separation, surface subpanels, and test-tube absorption behavior differ substantially from the source.
action_items: Recreate the source as a fixed multipanel layout, or make the default linked overview match it without overlapping the color wheel, surface plate, and test tube.
Build panel (a) as four separate surface diagrams arranged 2x2, matching the black, transparent/outline, yellow reflecting, and yellow transmitting cases.
Make panel (c) front-facing and upright with the same incoming and outgoing ray counts as the source, removing orange/red transmitted rays for the blue-appearing solution.
Remove or reduce extra titles, markers, legends, and chemical annotations so the labels match the original figure more closely.

plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels — (a), (b), and (c) — that together explain how the selective absorption of visible light by a substance determines its perceived color. Panel (a) shows four flat surfaces interacting with multicolored arrows representing the full visible spectrum: the top-left black surface absorbs all incoming colored arrows and reflects none; the top-right white/gray surface reflects all incoming colors; the bottom-left yellow surface absorbs most colors and reflects only yellow; and the bottom-right yellow surface absorbs the complementary color (indigo) from white light, also appearing yellow, illustrating that a color can arise either from selective reflection or from complementary-color absorption. Panel (b) is a color wheel divided into pie-shaped sectors spanning from approximately 400 nm (violet) through 430 nm (blue-violet), 490 nm (cyan-green), 560 nm (yellow-green), 580 nm (yellow), 620 nm (orange-red), and 800 nm (red), with colors arranged so that complementary pairs sit directly across the wheel from each other. Panel (c) depicts a test tube containing a blue [Cu(NH3)4]2+ solution: a full set of colored arrows labeled "White light" enters from the left, the orange and red arrows are absorbed by the solution, and the remaining arrows — violet, blue, cyan, green, and yellow — emerge on the right as "Blue-appearing light." This figure motivates the use of the complementary color wheel to predict what color a transition-metal complex will appear based on which wavelengths its d–d or charge-transfer transitions absorb.

demo_steps.title: Absorption on the wheel
demo_steps.narration: Start on the color wheel with absorption near 620 nm, in the orange-red region. The marker opposite it indicates the complementary blue/cyan appearance.

demo_steps.title: Colored surface
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the surface panel. For a colored yellow-appearing surface, most colors are absorbed while yellow-related light is reflected toward the viewer.

demo_steps.title: Black, white, and transparent limits
demo_steps.narration: Changing the surface type shows the limiting cases: black absorbs all visible bands, white reflects them all, and a transparent material transmits them through the plate.

demo_steps.title: Blue-appearing solution
demo_steps.narration: In the test tube, orange-red absorption removes those wavelengths from white light. The transmitted mixture is dominated by shorter wavelengths and appears blue.

demo_steps.title: Linked comparison
demo_steps.narration: The overview shows the same selected wavelength driving all panels together: highlighted sector on the wheel, absorption/reflection on the surface, and transmitted color through the solution.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Overall scene should preserve the textbook layout but use a tabbed/panel view by default: panel (b) centered first, with optional linked overview arranging (a) left, (b) upper right, and (c) lower center. Use orthographic/axonometric styling with no strong perspective convergence. Panel (a): one active tilted rectangular plate about 3.2 × 2.0 world units, lying in the XZ plane with +X screen-right and +Z receding up-right; plate corners form a parallelogram like the source. Incoming arrows are parallel colored lines about 2.4 units long, slanting from left/front toward the plate, ordered top-to-bottom violet #4b00ff, blue #1e3cff, cyan #49e6e6, green #33ff00, yellow #ffe600, orange #ff7a00, red #ff0000. Arrowheads point into the plate. Reflected arrows bend at the plate and travel up-right/back-right; transmitted arrows continue through in the same direction for the transparent case. Plate colors: black absorbing #000000; white reflecting #f5f5f5 with gray outline #808080; transparent plate pale gray/white with opacity about 0.25 and gray outline; colored surface pale yellow #ffff66 with gray outline. Colored-surface behavior should by default show yellow/orange-green reflected for yellow appearance and the complementary absorbed wavelength highlighted according to the slider. Panel (b): circular color wheel radius about 1.35 units, flat in screen plane. Divide into approximate sectors following the source labels: 400 nm violet at left-upper-left, 430 nm blue-violet at lower-left, 490 nm cyan at bottom, 560 nm green/yellow-green at lower-right, 580 nm yellow at right-upper-right, 620 nm orange-red at top, 800 nm red at upper-left. Complementary colors lie diametrically opposite; selected wavelength angle should interpolate continuously around this wheel rather than jump only at labels. Use black outlines #000000, label text black. Panel (c): test tube centered vertically, glass cylinder about 0.75 units wide and 3.1 units tall with rounded bottom and elliptical rim; glass pale cyan #b7d9d9 at 0.35 opacity, outlines #88b6b6. Liquid fills lower about 2.2 units, blue #3f86ff with slight vertical gradient and opacity about 0.75. Incoming arrows on left are horizontal, length about 2.0 units, stacked vertically with same visible-spectrum colors, arrowheads pointing right into tube. Outgoing arrows on right are horizontal, length about 2.1 units, with absorbed wavelength and neighboring band attenuated or absent; for wavelength 620 nm, suppress red/orange and leave violet/blue/cyan/green/yellow so the label reads 'Blue-appearing light'. Text labels are black sans-serif and placed as in the source: 'White light' above left bundle and apparent-color label above right bundle.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement the three panels as grouped objects that can be shown/hidden by panelView; in Linked overview scale each group down and place them in the source-like arrangement. The wavelength slider should update a single shared selectedWavelength state: move the color-wheel marker, recolor/brighten the matching arrow, compute complementary apparent hue by adding 180 degrees on the wheel, and update the test-tube liquid and outgoing-arrow mixture. For the click interaction, raycast color wheel sectors and set selectedWavelength to that sector center. Use emissive or high-saturation materials for arrows so the spectrum remains vivid against white background. Render arrows as THREE.Line or TubeGeometry shafts with cone arrowheads; use dashed or fading segments inside surfaces/tube to indicate absorption. Keep all labels as screen-facing sprites or CSS2D text for readability.
